extracted.intended_audience: publishers, journal editors, and the research community (authors and reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for how journal peer review should operate, what it should achieve (purposes such as soundness, originality, fit, and improvement), roles and responsibilities of editors/reviewers/publishers, and assessments of emerging models (open review, post-publication review, third-party platforms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review: soundness (fundamental purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Check the work for ‘soundness’: has the research been performed to reasonable standards, and are the findings and the conclusions drawn from them in that sense valid?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as the first and fundamental purpose; underpins mega-journals that treat soundness as sole criterion. Includes ensuring basic technical and ethical standards, reproducibility and that experiments/studies can be independently reproduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review: originality, significance and broader interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the originality, significance and broader interest of the research: is it new and of wider significance and interest rather than another example of a well-known finding?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often used by selective/high-status journals to filter for high-impact work; more subjective than soundness. Helps determine selection for higher-status journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review: fit with the journal
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the ‘fit’ with the journal to which a paper has been submitted: is the paper likely to be of interest to the readers of this particular journal?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection criterion distinct from soundness; important for editors and varies by journal scope and audience. Used to justify cascade/transfer decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review: help authors improve their paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide feedback to authors on how the paper might be enhanced so that it maximises credit and rewards for authors and the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associated especially with high-status journals; can be time-consuming but often improves presentation, identifies errors and enhances accuracy and significance. Balance needed to avoid excessive, dispiriting demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and reliability of data
rubrics_metrics.description: Published experiments/studies should be capable of being reproduced by someone working independently; peer review should help ensure reproducibility and reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report highlights high irreproducibility in some fields (e.g. biomedical). Publishers implement checks and initiatives (e.g. Nature reproducibility efforts); review should include checks on methods, data access and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and openness of review
rubrics_metrics.description: Move towards greater transparency and openness in the review process, distinguishing between revealing reviewers’ identities and revealing the content of reviews to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community acceptability varies by discipline; identity disclosure may be less acceptable than making review content public. Many innovations are being piloted or optional to avoid alienating communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction and dialogue between editors, reviewers and authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage more interaction between editors, reviewers and authors and potentially with post-publication commenters and raters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greater interaction may improve review quality but some editorial management systems do not facilitate it. New end-to-end platforms may enable dialogue if they do not unduly increase burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article-level metrics and altmetrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide article-level metrics beyond views, downloads and citations to include metrics for comments, ratings, social media mentions, news mentions and bookmarking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Services like Altmetric, Plum Analytics, Impact Story provide these; debate about generation, weighting and aggregation. Metrics may reduce reliance on journal impact factors if properly designed and interpreted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition, credit and rewards for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide scholarly credit, recognition and accreditation for reviewers’ contributions rather than monetary rewards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start-ups (Publons, Peerage of Science) and publishers are exploring recognition systems; community views differ on CV value. Little enthusiasm for direct monetary payment; indirect rewards (discounts) occasionally discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training, guidance and feedback for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve guidance, training, feedback and assessment for reviewers to sustain confidence in peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes development of templates, feedback loops to reviewers, and monitoring of reviewer performance. House of Commons and other bodies have highlighted importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate purposes: soundness vs significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between assessing whether research is sound (worthy of publication) and whether it fits the nature, scope and ambitions of a particular journal (significance/impact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to reduce redundant effort when papers move between journals; supports cascade/transfer systems and mega-journal models. Not always clear-cut in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors’ responsibilities and quality oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors take the final publication decision, set journal policy, select reviewers, assess potentially conflicting reports and ensure the system operates effectively and fairly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting appropriate reviewers, avoiding bias, monitoring review quality, providing feedback to authors, managing editorial boards, and ensuring triage and baseline quality thresholds are applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers’ responsibilities and expected conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should recommend (not decide) publication, treat manuscripts in confidence, declare conflicts of interest, avoid unfair advantage from privileged information, and typically use a standard review template.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are expected to be constructive and avoid ad hominem or unethical practices (e.g., delaying to gain precedence). COPE guidance applies for misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher/editorial staff pre-review checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial staff check that submissions fall within scope and meet journal policies (format, research ethics, authorship contributions, nomenclature codes, links to underlying data, etc.) and run plagiarism/image-manipulation checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many journals use submission/tracking systems (Editorial Manager, ScholarOne, OJS). Staff may perform triage to ensure baseline standards before sending for full peer review; failing checks can return paper to authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triage and baseline threshold for full peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial editorial triage aims to ensure only papers meeting a baseline threshold of quality and relevance proceed to full peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highly selective journals may reject many at this stage. Triage reduces reviewer burden and speeds process but must be applied judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficacy as quality control (detecting flawed or fraudulent work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review should function effectively as a quality control mechanism to detect errors, flawed methods, misconduct, fraud and prevent publication of invalid work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence shows peer review is imperfect; retractions and post-publication corrections indicate gaps. Publishers need additional checks (plagiarism, image forensics) and vigilance to prevent scams (bogus reviews).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and bias mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and mitigate unfairness and bias (sex, race, nationality, institutional prestige, field) that can influence editorial and reviewer judgements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include double-blind review, open review, and editor oversight. Publishers have taken steps to reduce bias; COPE provides guidance on handling ethical breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication bias and diversity of publishable outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid systematic bias against negative results, replications, interdisciplinary work, or unusual findings that might be suppressed by conservative review judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mega-journals that focus on soundness help address some publication bias. For interdisciplinary work, journals may increase number of reviewers to cover multiple perspectives; editors should be mindful of double-jeopardy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing subversions and reviewer fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Guard against exploitation of editorial systems (e.g., bogus reviews submitted via author-suggested reviewers) and other subversions that compromise review integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enhance reviewer-selection checks, disable or vet author-suggested reviewer nomination, improve system security and verification of reviewer identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variants of peer review (identity disclosure and timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different models include single-blind (reviewers anonymous), double-blind (both anonymous), open review (identities revealed), pre-publication vs post-publication review, and interactive review models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each variant has trade-offs in bias, acceptability across communities, and feasibility. Many publishers pilot optional approaches; cultural differences across disciplines influence uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication review, comments and ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms for post-publication commentary, reviews and ratings that allow continued scrutiny and assessment of a published article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linking pre- and post-publication activity is desirable but technically/logistically challenging. Some platforms assign DOIs to reviews and versions; publishers provide limited linkages to post-publication activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent and third-party peer review platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Third-party services (e.g., Peerage of Science, Publons, Libre/Open Scholar) provide independent review, reviewer ratings, and options to expose reviews to publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful especially for mega-journals or pre-submission review; publishers are cautious about outsourcing core review because of journal-specific selection criteria and editorial control concerns. Services may offer 'select' or 'connect' integrations with publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardised signalling of peer review (metadata and badges)
rubrics_metrics.description: Services like PRE-val aim to gather tagged metadata about the peer review process and provide badges/signals that an article underwent peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeks to verify for end users that articles have been peer reviewed and provide information about the nature of the process; uptake by publishers remains limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment, rating and scoring of reviews and reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems to assess the quality of individual reviews and to rate reviewers (via editorial monitoring, third-party platforms or feedback from authors/editors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peerage of Science and others implement multi-stage review scoring and reviewer ratings; publishers monitor review samples and may survey participants to provide feedback and identify training needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-effectiveness and timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review should be efficient, cost-effective and timely, minimising unnecessary delays and hidden costs to reviewers, editors, publishers and researchers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise significant hidden/unpaid costs; repeated review cycles and transfers increase time and cost. Approaches to reduce delays include transferring reviews, cascade systems, and exploring post-publication models where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workload balance and reviewer recruitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure fair distribution of reviewing workload and effective recruitment of qualified reviewers across geographic and disciplinary communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of geographic imbalance in reviewing; publishers should track workloads, diversify reviewer pools and avoid overburdening willing reviewers. Systems may take reviewer workload and track record into account when selecting reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive vs over-critical reviewing (tone and demands)
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage reviews that are constructive and supportive rather than purely negative or making unreasonable demands on authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should exert influence to guide reviewers toward constructive feedback; overly critical reviews can be dispiriting and counter-productive, particularly in fast-moving fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling authorship, contributorship and ethical declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Require clear statements about named authors' contributions, adherence to research ethics, and compliance with nomenclature or field-specific codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers and editorial staff check for authorship criteria (ICMJE, CSE) and ethical compliance during submission; failures are returned for correction. Such checks support transparency and accountability.
